results.q: What is CPU scheduling?
results.answer: CPU scheduling is the operating system's decision about which process in the ready queue gets the CPU next. Because a process alternates between CPU bursts and I/O bursts, the CPU would sit idle during I/O if nothing else could run. The scheduler keeps the CPU busy by switching to another ready process whenever the running one blocks, finishes, or is preempted. The goal is to maximise CPU utilisation and throughput while minimising waiting time, turnaround time and response time.

results.q: Why is CPU scheduling necessary?
results.answer: CPU scheduling is needed because the CPU is much faster than I/O devices and there are usually more ready processes than CPUs. results.q: What is a context switch?
results.answer: A context switch is the act of saving the state of the currently running process and loading the saved state of the next process to run. Context switches happen whenever the scheduler moves the CPU from one process to another, for example when a Round Robin quantum expires. They are pure overhead: no user work is done during the switch, so systems try to keep them infrequent.

results.q: What is SJF?
results.answer: Shortest Job First schedules the ready process with the smallest next CPU burst. results.q: What is aging in CPU scheduling?
results.answer: Aging is a technique that gradually raises the priority of a process the longer it waits in the ready queue. A low-priority process can be bypassed repeatedly if higher-priority processes keep arriving or stay ready, so it may wait indefinitely. This can happen in both preemptive and non-preemptive Priority scheduling, depending on the workload. The usual mitigation is aging: the priority of a process is raised gradually the longer it waits, so eventually even a low-priority process becomes the highest-priority one and gets the CPU.

results.q: Write a short note on Round Robin scheduling.
results.answer: Round Robin (RR) serves a circular FIFO ready queue and gives each process at most one time quantum before moving it to the tail. It is preemptive: a timer interrupt takes the CPU when the quantum expires. results.q: In one line, what is the formula for waiting time?
results.answer: Waiting time = turnaround time − burst time, which is the same as completion time − arrival time − burst time. It is the total time a process spends in the ready queue.
